title: Repair mechanical slips in code
statement: Repair in code what needs no judgment, such as quotation marks missing round the text's exact words, and send back to the writer only what does.
example: On 2 of 2 new texts, the debate block's last draft failed for missing quotation marks alone and never reached the judge.
detail: The lesson engine gives a failing draft one correction pass with the reasons, and it already repairs some slips in code: it drops a leading verdict, replaces a semicolon or dash standing in for a comma, and renames 'paragraph b' to 'Answer B'. Its debate block requires each push-back to quote the text, which code reads as words inside quotation marks. On a poem and a speech the last drafts' push-backs used the text's exact words without the marks, so after 2 tries both blocks failed on that check alone, with 0 judge calls, though code that finds the text's exact words could have marked them.
against: Whether the repaired drafts would have passed is unknown: the first judged drafts did quote the text, and the judge failed one push-back on the poem (0.39, `g9-transformer-runs/decisions/f23aebacf033daa2.json`, lines 119-122) and was unsure of both on the speech (0.52 and 0.51, `g9-transformer-runs/decisions/aeb043df247f1b45.json`, lines 85-88 and 123-126).

evidence.quote: judge checks the rest on positive evidence, and a failing draft gets exactly one correction pass with the reasons.
the animated build's punctuation (no semicolon or dash standing in for a comma)
leading verdict ("Correct.", "This is incorrect;") is dropped: both builds show the verdict themselves (YES, NOT THAT
the reader sees "Answer A" and "Answer B", so the feedback names them that way ("paragraph b" -> "Answer B")
check("counters-quote", "Each push-back quotes the text", item.sides.every((s) => quotesIn(s.counter).length > 0), "a push-back quotes no words from the text"),
How do the details of a wrinkled lip and sneer of cold command suggest a ruler who also possessed great passion?
"counter": "How can speech matter if the world will little note, nor long remember what we say here?"
"counter_1": "How do you explain the claim that \"the world will little note, nor long remember what we say here\"?"
Rewritten rather than rejected. A reply with a dash in it is a good reply with a dash in it, and a child waiting on an answer is not served by it being thrown away and re-asked for.
